Pate
PAYT
noun
Of uncertain origin, in Middle English pate, “the head, the crown or top of the head, the skull”; hence the scalp or crown. A KJV word occurring but once, at the end of the seventh psalm.

Biblical Definition

A pate is the crown or top of the head — the skull, the scalp, the very summit of a man. The word stands once in Scripture, and it stands at the end of a psalm about justice: “His mischief shall return upon his own head, and his violent dealing shall come down upon his own pate” (Psa 7:16). David has been describing the wicked man at his work: he travails with iniquity, conceives mischief, brings forth falsehood; “He made a pit, and digged it, and is fallen into the ditch which he made” (Psa 7:15). The picture is of a man labouring hard at his own destruction — digging with sweat and care, and tumbling in. The pate is where the whole thing lands. Not on the innocent he hunted, not on some distant generation, but squarely on the top of his own head, in the exact measure he intended for another. This is not fate or irony; it is the government of God, who has ordained that sin be paid its wages. Solomon says the same: “Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein: and he that rolleth a stone, it will return upon him” (Pro 26:27), and Paul seals it: “God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap” (Gal 6:7). The pit-digger’s pate is the plainest doctrine of retribution in the Psalter, and the psalm ends not in gloating but in praise of the LORD’s righteousness.

Webster 1828 Definition

The head; the crown or top of the head; the scalp. In Psalm 7 the place where the violent man’s own dealing lands.

PATE, the head; the top of the head; the skull or scalp.

In Middle English pate, of uncertain origin, used commonly of the crown.

A KJV word occurring but once (Psa 7:16).

The violent man’s dealing comes down upon his own pate.

It figures the just retribution of God upon the sinner’s own head.

Key Scripture

Psa 7:16 — "His mischief shall return upon his own head, and his violent dealing shall come down upon his own pate."

Psa 7:15 — "He made a pit, and digged it, and is fallen into the ditch which he made."

Pro 26:27 — "Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein: and he that rolleth a stone, it will return upon him."

Gal 6:7 — "Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap."

Modern Corruption

Not a contested doctrine but the old word for the crown of the head; it recovers the government of a God who is not mocked and pays every man his own measure.

expand to see more

The live misuse is to read this psalm as a proverb about consequences and nothing more — a piece of worldly wisdom about how bad choices catch up with people. That drains it. David is not observing a pattern; he is confessing a Judge. “God judgeth the righteous, and God is angry with the wicked every day” is the same psalm. The pit does not swallow the digger by accident of physics; the LORD, who tries the hearts and reins, brings the man’s mischief back upon his own pate in the very measure he had prepared for his neighbour. Take God out of the seventh psalm and you are left with a superstition; leave Him in, and you have justice.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God is not mocked. A man may dig his pit in secret, roll his stone uphill in confidence, and reckon that the poor and the upright have no avenger — and every stroke of the spade is a stroke against his own skull. Whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap; the harvest is certain and the measure is exact. Yet mark how David ends: not with a laugh at the fallen but with worship — “I will praise the LORD according to his righteousness.” The saint takes no pleasure in the pate that is struck. He praises the God who governs, and he keeps his own hands from the spade.

The word means the head, the crown or top of the head, the scalp.
